content: Schizophrenia is a severe mental health disorder that affects over 21 million individuals globally, as reported by the World Health Organization in 2015. It accounts for approximately 1.8% of global years lived with disability (YLDs), according to Vos in 2013. The symptoms of schizophrenia are categorized into three main groups: positive symptoms, such as hallucinations, delusions, and thought disorders; negative symptoms, including blunted affect, lack of motivation, and social withdrawal; and cognitive symptoms, such as a decline in the ability to learn new information. Individuals with schizophrenia experience significantly higher mortality rates, up to 50% greater than the general population. This increased mortality is attributed to various comorbid medical conditions and a heightened risk of suicide, with an estimated lifetime suicide risk of 5% in adults with schizophrenia. The disorder also profoundly impacts quality of life, as individuals often face challenges related to social interactions, employment, and housing, in addition to managing their diagnosis. Schizophrenia is diagnosed using established diagnostic systems, the most widely used being the International Classification of Disease (ICD) and the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM). According to the DSM, a diagnosis of schizophrenia requires the presence of symptoms for at least six months, with at least one month of active symptoms. Schizophrenia is considered a multifactorial disorder, as no single cause has been identified. Contributing factors include genetic predisposition, environmental influences such as obstetric complications, social isolation, lack of familial support, migrant status, and urban living conditions. Although there are numerous pharmacological and psychosocial therapies available for the treatment of schizophrenia, there is currently no cure. Most pharmacological treatments target the dopamine pathways in the brain, as research has shown that individuals with schizophrenia exhibit overactivity of dopamine in the central nervous system. Cariprazine is an orally administered atypical antipsychotic medication. It was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in September 2015 for the treatment of schizophrenia and for the acute management of manic or mixed episodes associated with bipolar I disorder. The initial dose of cariprazine is 1.5 mg on the first day, which can be increased to 3 mg on the second day. Subsequent dose adjustments can be made in increments of 1.5 to 3 mg, depending on the patient’s clinical response and tolerability. The recommended dosage range is 1.5 mg to 6 mg per day. Cariprazine is rapidly absorbed, with peak blood concentrations occurring three to four hours after administration in fasting patients. It accumulates with continued use, but its concentrations remain proportional to the dose within the effective range. The drug crosses the blood-brain barrier effectively, as demonstrated by a brain-to-plasma area under the curve (AUC) ratio of 7.6:1 in rodent studies. Cariprazine undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism via the cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzyme system, primarily CYP3A4 and, to a lesser extent, CYP2D6. Its active metabolites, desmethyl-cariprazine and didesmethyl-cariprazine, are produced during this metabolic process. The mean half-life of cariprazine is relatively long, ranging from two to five days for the parent compound and two to three weeks for didesmethyl-cariprazine. Consequently, patients are exposed to significantly higher levels of didesmethyl-cariprazine compared to cariprazine itself. Cariprazine has demonstrated efficacy in improving both the positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia. It is generally well-tolerated, with common adverse effects including akathisia, restlessness, tremor, back pain, and extrapyramidal symptoms. Most current antipsychotic medications primarily target dopamine D2 receptors, which are effective in alleviating positive symptoms but have little to no impact on negative or cognitive symptoms. In contrast, cariprazine is a potent partial agonist of dopamine D3 and D2 receptors, with a preference for binding to D3 receptors. It also exhibits partial agonist activity at serotonin 5-HT1A receptors. The therapeutic effects of cariprazine in reducing both positive and negative symptoms are believed to result from its ability to modulate overstimulated dopamine receptors. Given the complexity of schizophrenia treatment and the variability in patient responses to existing therapies, the development of new treatment options is highly valuable. The goal is to identify treatments that offer maximum efficacy while minimizing adverse effects. Therefore, it is essential to systematically evaluate the available data on cariprazine as a potential new and effective treatment for schizophrenia.
